summary: The machine has the Node.js runtime, az, the documentdb MCP server and a rich set of DocumentDB skills; a developer can start implementing the Node.js LlamaIndex agent and its aggregation tool against the live DocumentDB cluster. Several documentation confusions were found (the cold answers often mixed this service with Cosmos DB's Mongo API or upstream MongoDB), a few CLI tools and accelerators that would speed development are missing (mongosh, azd, DocumentDB Agent Kit), and a small set of required facts (LLM provider/model and exact collection/field names) remain unspecified and must be decided by the implementer before final polishing.
summary_points: Build can start: required runtimes and a data-plane MCP server (documentdb) are available and connected to the cluster; Node.js + npm present.
Key DocumentDB skills are installed (driver, indexing, vector-search, connection, local-deployment) and the documentdb MCP toolkit is available for database verification.

Multiple cold answers were incorrect or outdated because they described Azure Cosmos DB (Mongo API) or upstream MongoDB rather than Azure DocumentDB; these must be corrected in the sample's README and prompt templates.
Missing accelerators that would speed work: DocumentDB Agent Kit (skill) and local mongosh on PATH; both are easy to add but not blocking.
Verdict: ready_with_gaps — proceed, but pick LLM provider/model, collection/field names, and seed-data size; install optional tools to make verification and local dev smoother.

tools.name: documentdb (MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Run aggregation pipelines, create/list indexes, sample documents, run explain() and other data-plane verification against the live Azure DocumentDB cluster.
tools.detail: MCP server 'documentdb' present in inventory with data-plane tools (aggregate, create_index, list_indexes, explain_operation, sample_documents, insert_documents, etc.).
tools.impact_if_missing: Can't inspect the live cluster or verify indexes and query plans programmatically; would need manual portal work or direct driver connections.
tools.workaround: Use the mongodb Node driver to run the same aggregation commands against the cluster (requires DOCUMENTDB_URI), or use the Azure portal Connection strings pane for manual checks.

references.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Node.js

tools.name: learn (Microsoft Learn docs search)
tools.needed_for: Authoritative grounding of API, resource types, connection strings, vector and full-text search syntax, and feature flags used in the sample.
tools.detail: learn_microsoft_docs_search available and used to fetch Microsoft Learn pages for DocumentDB.
tools.impact_if_missing: Lack of authoritative doc references; model answers couldn't be verified.
tools.workaround: Rely on local skill docs or cached resources, but verification is weaker.

references.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB

tools.name: az (Azure CLI)
tools.needed_for: Inspecting resource groups, reading cluster resource properties, toggling preview features if needed, or retrieving portal-provided connection strings (if not using only DOCUMENTDB_URI).
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to read cluster-level properties and feature flags programmatically; some portal-only steps would be manual.
tools.workaround: Use the Azure portal for the same checks, or rely on the documentdb MCP server for data-plane operations.

tools.name: node / npm / npx
tools.needed_for: Build and run the Node.js LlamaIndex agent, install packages, run seed script, and execute demo CLI or HTTP server.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run the sample or install packages.
tools.workaround: Install Node.js and npm; but inventory shows they are present.

tools.name: docker
tools.needed_for: Optional: run the local DocumentDB gateway image for development if you prefer local integration tests instead of the live cluster.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run the official local gateway image; must test directly against live cluster.
tools.workaround: Test directly against the live cluster (DOCUMENTDB_URI) as described in the prompt_md.

references.title: Development loop (DocumentDB local gateway) - docker run on port 10260

tools.name: mongosh
tools.needed_for: Interactive checks of connectivity, indexes and small ad-hoc queries during development; helpful when verifying example aggregation pipelines by hand.
tools.detail: mongosh not found on PATH per inventory.
tools.impact_if_missing: Developer will lack an interactive shell for quick manual checks; verification still possible programmatically (Node driver or MCP server), but slower for ad-hoc debugging.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server aggregate/find tools or use a small Node.js script that calls the MongoDB driver to run queries. To install, add mongosh to PATH (e.g. npm i -g mongosh or install from MongoDB downloads).

references.title: Quickstart: Evaluate DocumentDB on Azure Local (connect with mongosh)

tools.name: documentdb-driver (skill)
tools.needed_for: Driver initialization best practices: singleton MongoClient, pool settings and example code for Node.js driver usage with Azure DocumentDB.
tools.impact_if_missing: Risk of writing non-recommended driver usage patterns (e.g., opening/closing clients per request) causing connection pool exhaustion.
tools.workaround: Follow official mongodb driver docs for Node.js and the documentdb-driver guidance in the repository. Use a process-wide MongoClient singleton.

tools.name: documentdb-connection (skill)
tools.needed_for: Connection tuning details (timeouts, socket options, pooling) and troubleshooting connection errors the sample may encounter when connecting from the example process environment.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to pick conservative but correct defaults for maxPoolSize, socketTimeoutMS, and maxIdleTimeMS; possible intermittent connection problems during demos.
tools.workaround: Use the connection guidance in the Azure docs (set maxIdleTimeMS, socketTimeoutMS) and example connection strings in portal docs.

references.title: Troubleshoot common issues in Azure DocumentDB

tools.name: documentdb-indexing (skill)
tools.needed_for: Guidance to pick the compound index {customerId:1, timestamp:1} and any covering indexes the sample needs for match+sort performance.
tools.impact_if_missing: May pick suboptimal indexes or omit guidance on index write costs.
tools.workaround: Follow examples in the Azure docs for creating compound indexes and use the documentdb MCP explain tool to verify index usage.

tools.name: documentdb-local-deployment (skill)
tools.needed_for: Local development guidance, local gateway Docker image port and TLS defaults, and advice for seed scripts and dev/prod parity.
tools.impact_if_missing: Developer might not follow local gateway best practices (port 10260, tlsAllowInvalidCertificates for local) or produce an idempotent seed script.
tools.workaround: Read the quickstart and use Docker image ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest; or test against live cluster as run policy suggests.

tools.name: documentdb-vector-search (skill)
tools.needed_for: If the sample uses vector search (for RAG or hybrid retrieval), provides correct create-index syntax (DiskANN/HNSW/IVF) and $search pipeline usage.
tools.impact_if_missing: Wrong vector-index creation or incorrect query shape leading to runtime errors or poor performance.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb vector-search docs (cosmosSearch operator and cosmosSearchOptions) and the MCP create_index tool.

references.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB

accelerators_missed: DocumentDB Agent Kit (not installed). Install with: npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit
mongosh (not on PATH). Install mongosh or use the system package (e.g., npm i -g mongosh or use MongoDB's installer) to speed interactive checks.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (the same resource type used for Cosmos DB accounts exposing MongoDB endpoints).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB clusters are represented using the resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep/Terraform docs)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared resource provider namespace and long-standing usage of Microsoft.DocumentDB for Cosmos-like MongoDB APIs; older Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) resource types look similar and were historically used for the Mongo API.

confusion_sources.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (uses databaseAccounts)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder used databaseAccounts in ARM/Bicep/Terraform, they would target the wrong resource type and deployment would fail or apply to Cosmos DB resources rather than the vCore DocumentDB mongoClusters resource.
improvements: Update the top-level 'create a cluster' quickstart to call out the exact ARM/Bicep/Terraform resource Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and add a note contrasting it with Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.
Add a deprecation or distinction note to pages that still mention databaseAccounts when referring to the vCore-managed DocumentDB offering.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example to create: az cosmosdb create ... This is in the core az CLI (no extra extension required).
confusions.grounded_answer: Current command surface includes az cosmosdb mongocluster commands (e.g., az cosmosdb mongocluster create). The CLI group is 'az cosmosdb' with a 'mongocluster' subgroup; historically some features lived in extensions but current docs show built-in subcommands for mongocluster.

grounding_links.title: az cosmosdb mongocluster create (Azure CLI docs)
Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM docs)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The 'az cosmosdb' command group historically managed Cosmos DB databaseAccounts and the older Mongo API, causing overlap and confusion; some older guides described extension-based CLI flows.

confusion_sources.title: Older az cosmosdb quickstarts and Cosmos DB docs (showing databaseAccounts usage)

confusions.build_risk: Using an incorrect CLI command or extension could fail to create the intended resource type (mongocluster) or invoke the wrong subcommand; the builder may try an obsolete extension command flow.
improvements: Add a short 'Which CLI command creates a DocumentDB cluster' note to the mongoClusters Learn page that shows az cosmosdb mongocluster create and points to the right CLI subgroup explicitly.
Mark any older quickstarts that use databaseAccounts with a banner explaining the newer 'mongocluster' resource type and command.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts ... Terraform: azurerm_cosmosdb_account ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Bicep/ARM and Terraform should target the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource (and the azapi/bicep AVM modules for Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)); the older databaseAccounts / azurerm_cosmosdb_account refer to Cosmos DB accounts not the vCore DocumentDB mongoClusters resource.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep/Terraform docs)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Earlier Cosmos DB guidance used Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts and provider-specific Terraform resources; the newer vCore offering uses a separate 'mongoClusters' resource shape.

confusion_sources.title: Terraform / Azurerm references for Cosmos DB account (older pattern)

confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts / azurerm_cosmosdb_account in templates will not create the intended vCore mongoClusters resource; provisioning/automation will fail or create a different service.
improvements: Add explicit Bicep / Terraform examples for Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters on the 'create cluster' quickstart page and call out that azurerm_cosmosdb_account is for the Cosmos DB (RU) path, not vCore DocumentDB.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical Cosmos connection example: mongodb://...@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB cluster (the vCore product) uses a different host suffix and port pattern: SRV-style 'mongodb+srv://<cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com' and the DocumentDB gateway default port is 10260 for non-SRV/gateway connections; when 'query from any node' is enabled per-node ports start at 10260 and increment. TLS (tls=true/ssl=true) is required. (Cosmos DB's mongo API uses *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com and port 10255.)

grounding_links.title: Query from any node in Azure DocumentDB (ports start at 10260)
Enable private access in Azure DocumentDB (connection strings & hostnames)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) endpoints (mongo.cosmos.azure.com, port 10255). Azure DocumentDB (vCore) uses mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com and port 10260 for its gateway and per-node ports.

confusion_sources.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (10255 example)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix/port breaks connectivity (connection refused or the driver hitting a different service) and can cause puzzling auth or protocol errors.
improvements: On the top-level connection guidance page, add a short table contrasting DocumentDB (mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com, 10260) vs Cosmos DB for MongoDB (mongo.cosmos.azure.com, 10255) with example connection strings.
Ensure sample .env.example templates specify DOCUMENTDB_URI and show the correct mongocluster SRV example for DocumentDB.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Either RUs (Cosmos) or vCore-based tiers (M30); if you see M30 expect vCore-based billing.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore clusters) is billed by compute tier (vCores) and storage — there are cluster tiers (M10, M20, M30, etc.). It does not use RU-based billing. This differs from Cosmos DB's request-unit model.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained (compute tiers and vCores)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed the two offerings: Cosmos DB flavors use RUs, while the vCore-based DocumentDB offering uses tiers named like M30 (vCores).

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) docs (RU model)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumed RU billing, they might choose the wrong terraform/Bicep resource or try to set RU throughput parameters that don't apply. The sample should document that the live cluster uses M30/vCore billing.
improvements: Add explicit billing model note in the quickstart and 'create cluster' pages clarifying: 'This offering is vCore tiered (Mxx) billed by compute + storage — not RU-based Cosmos DB'.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary auth is SCRAM (username/password); AD (Entra) is generally not supported for Mongo drivers.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB native (SCRAM) authentication and also Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC/MONGODB-OIDC) flows for interactive and managed-identity scenarios; the docs provide an OIDC connection string sample using MONGODB-OIDC and guidance to register and use managed identities.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Many managed Mongo offerings historically lacked direct Azure AD/OIDC integration; the cold answer assumed that pattern. Azure DocumentDB explicitly documents OIDC/MONGODB-OIDC support and managed-identity registration steps.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes Entra ID is not supported they may not implement the recommended passwordless/managed-identity demo flows or omit RBAC examples; the sample should include both SCRAM examples and an optional OIDC/managed-identity example.
improvements: Add an OIDC/manged-identity example snippet to the Node quickstart and to the 'how to connect' page so builders see both SCRAM and Microsoft Entra ID flows.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the official MongoDB driver (mongodb npm package); no special DocumentDB SDK.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use the official MongoDB drivers (Node.js 'mongodb' package) to talk to Azure DocumentDB. There is no special separate service SDK for application code that accesses the Mongo API; use Mongo drivers and follow DocumentDB driver best practices.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Node.js

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Use createIndex with { embedding: 'vector' } and options algorithm:'hnsw' or 'ivf' ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports DiskANN, HNSW, and IVF vector indexes; index creation uses either the createIndexes API (with key: cosmosSearch and cosmosSearchOptions for vector indexes) or dedicated examples in the vector-search docs. Example forms use cosmosSearchOptions (kind: 'vector-hnsw' / 'vector-ivf' / 'vector-diskann') and parameters such as dimensions, numLists, m, efConstruction, lBuild and lSearch depending on algorithm.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB - create vector indexes and cosmosSearchOptions
Vector search examples (IVF HNSW DiskANN)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used an upstream MongoDB-style createIndex vector field, whereas Azure DocumentDB exposes vector indexing via a service-specific 'cosmosSearch' / cosmosSearchOptions construct and dedicated createIndexes/createIndex variants.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder tries to create vector indexes with upstream MongoDB syntax the operation will fail; they must use the DocumentDB vector index API (cosmosSearchOptions) and matching parameter names.
improvements: Add an explicit 'How to create a vector index' snippet in the quickstart and the Node vector-search quickstart showing cosmosSearchOptions for HNSW/IVF/DiskANN.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text searches are done by integrating with Azure Cognitive Search; hybrid vector+text should be done outside the DB.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB has an integrated full-text search engine (createSearchIndexes + $search) and integrated vector search (cosmosSearch). Hybrid search (BM25 + vector) is supported on the same cluster: create a BM25 search index with createSearchIndexes and a vector index with cosmosSearchOptions, then run separate aggregation pipelines and fuse results (server-side RRF via $unionWith or client-side fusion). You do not need an external Azure Cognitive Search index for BM25 + vector hybrid in DocumentDB.

grounding_links.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB (createSearchIndexes and $search)
Hybrid search (BM25 + vector) in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Some architectures use Azure Cognitive Search for advanced text capabilities; the cold answer assumed that external service is required. DocumentDB provides integrated BM25 search and hybrid fusion on-cluster.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cognitive Search integration pages (historic pattern for Cosmos DB solutions)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder wires their sample to an external search service they will add unnecessary complexity and extra ETL; they may also misdocument the sample and confuse users about on-cluster hybrid search capability.
improvements: Clarify on the 'full-text search' overview that DocumentDB provides integrated BM25 and vector search and give the hybrid RRF example alongside an optional note about integrating Azure Cognitive Search if a team prefers it for other reasons.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Newer clusters advertise MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol; some features like server-side JS and admin commands may be limited.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB advertises compatibility with MongoDB wire-protocol versions such as 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and newer as provided by the cluster's serverVersion property; the service documents feature compat and lists limitations (some admin commands, server-side JS, certain low-level admin features). Always check the cluster's 'serverVersion' and the DocumentDB 'compatibility features' docs for exact limits.

grounding_links.title: Moving from another MongoDB-compatible service to Azure DocumentDB (compatibility summary)
Migrate and compatibility / limitations pages

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer was cautious and generic; while it named 7.0 it missed the explicit list of supported versions and the official compatibility guidance; gaps came from conflating various offerings.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumed exact feature parity with a particular MongoDB server version they may use operators or commands not supported by the cluster; the sample must limit itself to documented supported features and include checks against cluster serverVersion if needed.
improvements: Add a short 'Driver compatibility and serverVersion' section to the quickstart that explains how to read the cluster's advertised serverVersion and link to the compatibility matrix.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: No official emulator; use local mongo:7.0 on 27017 — won't emulate provider-specific features.
confusions.grounded_answer: You can run the open-source DocumentDB gateway locally with the provided Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local) and the gateway listens on port 10260. This local DocumentDB image reproduces many provider features (gateway port 10260, TLS and admin options) and is recommended for development if you need feature parity; using generic mongo images won't emulate provider-specific vector/text features.

grounding_links.title: Development loop (DocumentDB local gateway) - docker run on port 10260
DocumentDB: The open-source engine powering Azure DocumentDB (running locally)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed there is no official local option and recommended vanilla MongoDB; while generic MongoDB is usable for simple unit tests, Microsoft provides a local DocumentDB gateway image that better mirrors the managed service (port 10260).
confusions.build_risk: Using mongo:latest for local dev will not reproduce DocumentDB vector/text or DocumentDB-specific connection semantics; tests that rely on those features will fail locally.
improvements: Add a 'run locally' section to the quickstart that shows the ghcr DocumentDB local image and the docker run example with port 10260 and TLS flags.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams are supported for MongoDB 3.6+; should be available via driver watch(); no special flag beyond replset/sharded deployment.
confusions.grounded_answer: Change streams are supported in Azure DocumentDB and the driver 'watch()' API is the correct approach; for multishard clusters a specific 'Change streams for multishard clusters' feature must be enabled in cluster Features. Also the service documents resumability and historical checkpoint options.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB (enable multi-shard change streams and usage)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed default availability across all cluster topologies; DocumentDB requires enabling a multi-shard change-stream preview feature for cross-shard aggregation of streams.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample assumes multi-shard change streams are always enabled, a demo that uses cluster-wide watch() across shards may fail until the feature is enabled; the builder should document the prerequisite and include a fallback (timestamp-based poll) in the seed/demo scripts.
improvements: Document the 'enable change streams for multishard clusters' step in the migration/quickstart and add a fallback code path that performs incremental polling if the feature is not available.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server profile (named documentdb) for data-plane tools; Azure MCP provides control-plane coverage.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the documentdb MCP server provides the DocumentDB data-plane tools (aggregate, create_index, explain, list_indexes, sample_documents, etc.); the general azure MCP server covers Azure control-plane operations but lacks the Mongo-aware explain/index viewers the documentdb server provides.

grounding_links.title: documentdb (MCP server) — available data-plane tools

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Microsoft had a service called DocumentDB which evolved into Azure Cosmos DB... the MongoDB-compatible offering is usually exposed as 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB API' or 'Azure managed MongoDB' depending on the SKU. The open-source DocumentDB project is unrelated.
confusions.grounded_answer: Confusing naming history: the original 'Azure DocumentDB' (2014) evolved into Azure Cosmos DB (the Core/SQL API). More recently, Microsoft released a vCore-based offering initially referred to as 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' and renamed/rebranded it as Azure DocumentDB (the current vCore-managed, MongoDB-compatible product), which is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine. The open-source DocumentDB project is related: the cloud service runs that engine. The relationships are subtle and have caused name collisions with 'Amazon DocumentDB'.

grounding_links.title: Moving from another MongoDB-compatible service to Azure DocumentDB (history and relation to Cosmos)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Multiple historical renames and overlapping names (DocumentDB, Cosmos DB, Cosmos DB for MongoDB vCore) lead to frequent confusion; the cold answer conflated the timelines and relationships.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample repository uses inconsistent naming (older 'Cosmos DB (vCore)' or 'DocumentDB' interchangeably) it will confuse readers; use the requested canonical name 'Azure DocumentDB' consistently and add a short note mentioning prior names.
improvements: Add a short 'Naming and history' section to the README explaining: 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore) was previously documented as Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore); older docs may still use that name. Do not confuse with Amazon DocumentDB.'

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Treat it as a Mongo server from the application's perspective and use standard MongoDB drivers; engine may be upstream MongoDB or a translation layer.
confusions.grounded_answer: Application code should use standard MongoDB drivers and treat the service as a Mongo endpoint, but the underlying engine is the DocumentDB open-source engine (not upstream MongoDB server), so some low-level features or admin operations may differ; builders must consult the compatibility matrix for subtle differences.

grounding_links.title: Moving from another MongoDB-compatible service to Azure DocumentDB (engine and compatibility)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer hedged answers between translation layers and upstream MongoDB; more precisely, DocumentDB runs the open-source DocumentDB engine beneath a Mongo-compatible wire-protocol surface, which matters for edge-case admin commands and some features.
confusions.build_risk: Relying on undocumented admin commands or assuming exact parity with a specific MongoDB server version may cause runtime failures; the sample should stick to documented Mongo API features and include a compatibility note.
improvements: Add a short compatibility note in the README and quickstart telling developers to check the cluster 'serverVersion' and the compatibility matrix before using advanced or admin-level features.

confusions.question: What index definition does this sample need for vector search?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a vector index on the embedding field with createIndex({embedding:'vector'}, { vector: { algorithm:'hnsw', dimensions:1536 } })
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB vector indexes are created with createIndexes / createIndex using a 'cosmosSearch' key or via a createIndexes template that sets cosmosSearchOptions (kind: 'vector-hnsw' / 'vector-ivf' / 'vector-diskann') and algorithm-specific parameters (dimensions, numLists, m, efConstruction, lBuild, etc.). The exact syntax uses cosmosSearchOptions rather than a generic embedding:'vector' option.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (create vector index examples and cosmosSearchOptions)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer attempted to use an upstream MongoDB-style vector index DSL; DocumentDB exposes vector indexing via service-specific cosmosSearchOptions.
confusions.build_risk: Attempting to create the vector index with upstream syntax will fail; the sample must use the DocumentDB vector index API so the vector search pipeline ($search + cosmosSearch) works.
improvements: Add a code snippet to the sample that creates the required vector index via the documentdb MCP create_index tool or shows the exact createIndexes JSON with cosmosSearchOptions.

confusions.question: What aggregation pipeline will the sample use to reconstruct a customer's journey (grouping and sorting)?
confusions.cold_answer: Pipeline: $match by customerId, $sort by timestamp, $group with $push of ordered events into events array, project timeline.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the recommended pipeline filters by customerId, sorts by timestamp, then groups (or projects) to collect an ordered array of events — e.g., [ { $match: {customerId: id} }, { $sort: { timestamp: 1 } }, { $group: { _id: '$customerId', events: { $push: { channel:'$channel', ts:'$timestamp', type:'$type', metadata:'$metadata' } } } }, { $project: { _id:0, customerId:'$_id', timeline: '$events' } } ].

grounding_links.title: Aggregation pipeline examples (group, push, sort) in DocumentDB docs

confusions.question: Which database should the sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the database named sample_customer_360_04 for all collections and indexes created by the sample.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the run environment specifies using database sample_customer_360_04 for sample artifacts.

grounding_links.title: Prompt run environment: sample_customer_360_04

confusions.question: How should the Node.js sample connect to the cluster at runtime?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it to the official mongodb driver.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use DOCUMENTDB_URI env var and the official mongodb driver; DO NOT write secrets to logs or files and provide .env.example with a placeholder.

grounding_links.title: Run environment: DOCUMENTDB_URI guidance (prompt skill_md)
Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Node.js (connection samples)

confusions.question: What client operation does the sample use to fetch changes or drive hybrid search/indexing?
confusions.cold_answer: Use collection.watch() change streams for streaming changes; if not available fallback to timestamp-based incremental poll.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: change streams (collection.watch()) are the preferred mechanism; if multi-shard change streams aren't enabled or not available, use timestamp-based incremental polling as a robust fallback.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB

information_gaps.title: LLM provider and model selection
information_gaps.description: The prompt asks for a LlamaIndex agent but does not specify which LLM provider, model names (for embeddings and generation), or environment variables (OPENAI_API_KEY, MODEL_NAME, AZURE_OPENAI endpoints) to use. I searched prompt_md and installed skills and found no authoritative instruction. The builder must choose and document models and embedding dims to ensure vector-index dimensions match.

information_gaps.title: Concrete collection/field names and event schema
information_gaps.description: The sample suggests 'touchpoint' or 'events' documents but does not fix the collection name or exact field names (customerId, timestamp, channel, eventType, metadata). I looked in the prompt_md and skills and found only a suggested shape in the prompt_review; the implementer must pick the exact schema and include it in seed scripts.

information_gaps.title: Seed data size and idempotency policy
